problem: RL object-goal navigation agents that inject a knowledge graph into the state or policy inflate the state space, which hurts sparse-reward learning. Their critics also estimate values poorly and give up early, before reaching the target.
motivation: Humans search for objects using prior knowledge of object co-location, adapt it to the new scene, and keep searching optimistically. Accurate value estimates lower gradient variance in actor-critic and give a better policy. Seeing a correlated object (e.g. a desk when looking for a book) should keep the estimated state value high.
key_idea: Use a learned object co-location graph (a Graph Transformer Network over visual and word-embedding node features) only in the critic, to add a graph-derived term to the value estimate, instead of feeding the graph to the actor or the state.
insight: Using the graph only as a value baseline beats putting it in the state (MAML-SS, which lowers SR and SPL) or in the policy (MAML-Action, which raises SR but drops SPL to 13.88). The gain depends on real prior knowledge, since random edge weights give SPL 15.32 / SR 40.5 versus 17.27 / 43.8. It also depends on visual node features: the language-only graph (Ours-LG) reaches only SPL 12.84. The value error plot shows GVE reduces error mainly on longer trajectories, where the LSTM forgets.
method: Prior knowledge graph: 89 object nodes and a 5-channel adjacency tensor (4 room-type channels plus a self-loop channel), with edges initialised from Visual Genome co-occurrence (at least 3 times). Node features are 512-d ResNet-18 observation features concatenated with 512-d GloVe embeddings of the object name.

Graph Transformer Network: learns soft-selected channel combinations H_i (softmax over channels) and multiplies M of them into A_NEW. Graph convolution over A_NEW+I then gives the graph embedding Q (512-d).

GVE critic: V(x_t)=W1·Q + W2·F(x_t,Z;θ), where F is the LSTM state encoder. The critic is partly separated from the actor, and the graph is used only for value estimation and trained with the value loss L_V.
A3C backbone: ResNet-18 features of 300x300 RGB plus a GloVe target embedding go into a 512-d LSTM, with a 6-way softmax actor and a scalar critic. Rewards are +5 for success and -0.01 per step.

MAML adaptation (from SAVN): a learned adaptation loss is used for test-time gradient updates. Meta-train uses sub-trajectories and meta-validation uses full trajectories, with SGD for the inner loop and Adam for the outer loop.
Ablation variants: MAML-SS (graph fed into the state), MAML-Action (graph fed into the policy), Ours-LG (language-only nodes), and Ours-RandomGraph (random edges).

setting.backbone: A3C actor-critic with ResNet-18 + GloVe + LSTM + GTN critic, trained with RL from scratch (ResNet-18 pre-trained)
setting.training_data: RL in AI2-THOR, 20 scenes per room type for training (5 val, 5 test), up to 7M episodes; graph edges initialised from Visual Genome co-occurrence
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (300x300) plus target object name as a GloVe embedding

numbers.extra: Visual Genome-initialised graph; 200 max test steps; SR/SPL also reported on episodes with optimal length >5 ('>5')

numbers_note: AI2-THOR object navigation is not in the canonical benchmark list, so it is labelled other. The test split is inferred from the setup (5 test scenes per room type). Per-room results are in Table 5 and were not extracted.
results: The full model (A3C+Graph+MAML+GVE) reaches SR 43.8 / SPL 17.27, beating the previous SOTA A3C+MAML (SAVN: SR 40.86 / SPL 16.15) by about 3 points SR and over 1 point SPL. The gain is larger on longer trajectories (SR>5 33.68 vs 28.70). It improves 3 of 4 room types over SAVN, with bedroom slightly worse.
limitations: Evaluated only in AI2-THOR with small scene splits, and only on top of A3C and MAML. Applicability to other actor-critic methods is hypothesised, not tested.
The graph needs a fixed object vocabulary (89 nodes) and Visual Genome priors, and it depends on visual node features.
Gains are modest, and one room type (bedroom) gets slightly worse.
